answers.question: For a fictional new sanitary drain in NYC, a two-inch horizontal pipe runs 20 feet and drops two inches uniformly. Is that enough fall?
answers.visibleAnswer:
Research complete
00:29

No. For horizontal drainage piping, a 2-inch pipe must slope at least 1/4 inch per foot; over 20 feet that is 5 inches of fall. Two inches is only 1/10 inch per foot, so it does not meet that minimum (2022 NYC Plumbing Code § 704.1).

answers.question: Correction: it is a four-inch pipe, and it drops three inches over that same 20-foot run. Does that satisfy the minimum slope?
answers.visibleAnswer:
Research complete
00:06

Yes. For a 4-inch horizontal drainage pipe, the minimum is 1/8 inch per foot; over 20 feet that requires 2.5 inches of fall. The proposed 3-inch drop exceeds the minimum (2022 NYC Plumbing Code § 704.1).

answers.question: On that same drain, can we reduce from four inches to three inches farther downstream because there is less room? This is the main horizontal line, not a toilet outlet connection.
answers.visibleAnswer:
Research complete
00:07

No. The pipe size cannot be reduced from 4 inches to 3 inches in the direction of flow; the 4-inch-by-3-inch allowance applies only to a water-closet connection, which you say this is not (2022 NYC Plumbing Code § 704.2). The 3-inch pipe’s minimum slope is 1/8 inch per foot, but meeting that slope would not permit reducing the main line’s diameter (§ 704.1).

No—not on the stated dimensions. Widening the path to 6 feet meets the minimum horizontal width, but 8 feet of clearance beneath the pipe is 1 foot short of the required 9-foot height. FC 504.4.4 allows a pipe to cross the path in accordance with FC 504.4.7, but that provision does not state that the 9-foot height minimum is reduced. (2022 NYC Fire Code §§ 504.4.4, 504.4.7.)

answers.question: Suppose we correct the overhead clearance to 9 feet and keep the path 6 feet wide. How much clear area must we leave at the rooftop bulkhead door?
answers.visibleAnswer:

Leave at least 6 feet of clearance in all directions from the bulkhead door opening, measured from the door hinge. This is a separate door-clearance requirement; the 6-foot-wide path and 9-foot overhead clearance do not replace it (2022 NYC Fire Code § 504.4.6).

answers.question: If this same fictional flat-roof building were revised from 85 feet to 110 feet high, would that rooftop-access provision still cover it? Please distinguish the limit of that provision from whether other access requirements could apply.
answers.visibleAnswer:
Research complete
00:23

Not under the ≤100-foot rooftop rule. At 110 feet, the building is outside FC 504.4’s height scope. But FC 504.5 separately addresses buildings more than 100 feet high: if constructed after that section’s effective date, they must have, to the maximum extent practicable, a path complying with FC 504.4.4 from rooftop access to the perimeter on any side with windows. That is a distinct, qualified requirement—not a conclusion that no rooftop-access requirements apply above 100 feet. (2022 NYC Fire Code §§ 504.4, 504.5.)

Will the fictional building be constructed after FC 504.5’s effective date? That determines whether its separate over-100-foot path requirement applies.

answers.question: For a fictional new gas-piping installation in an open outdoor yard in NYC, is 18 inches of earth cover above the top of the pipe enough? There are no protective steel plates, and the run is not underneath a building.
answers.visibleAnswer:
Research complete
00:42

No. For underground gas piping, the 2022 NYC Fuel Gas Code requires at least 24 inches of cover, measured from grade to the top of the pipe. Its stated exception allows less cover only with specified steel protective plates; without plates, 18 inches does not meet the stated minimum (FGC § 404.12). The separate rule for piping underground beneath buildings does not apply to your stated outdoor run (FGC § 404.14).

answers.question: Could protective steel plates let us keep that depth? If so, how would they have to be built and located?
answers.visibleAnswer:
Research complete
00:35

Yes. The 18-inch burial depth can be used if the underground piping system is protected by steel plates at least ¼ inch thick, with plate joints tack welded and overlapped by at least 3 inches; the pipe must be at least 4 inches below the protective plate (2022 NYC Fuel Gas Code § 404.12). The supplied rule does not specify plate width or how far plates must extend along the run.

answers.question: Separately, that gas line rises above ground outdoors in black steel. Can the exposed section remain bare, or does it need corrosion protection?
answers.visibleAnswer:
Research complete
00:40

No. The 2022 NYC Fuel Gas Code requires ferrous metal exposed outdoors to be protected against corrosion, so the exposed black-steel section cannot remain bare (FGC § 404.11.2). Permitted methods include galvanizing, bonded coatings, protective coatings, or protective wrappings; the referenced sections set approval and application conditions. In particular, bonded coatings are factory applied, except that field application is allowed per the manufacturer’s instructions where factory coating or wrapping was damaged or necessarily removed at joints (FGC §§ 404.11.4–404.11.6).

answers.question: For a fictional new office workroom in NYC, is a flat finished ceiling seven feet four inches above the finished floor high enough? This is not a basement or mezzanine, and there are no beams or dropped soffits.
answers.visibleAnswer:
